newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea won slumps to six-year lows.
newsitem.headline: South Korea won slumps to six-year lows.

text.p: South Korea's central bank defended the won on Wednesday with repeated rounds of intervention as the currency touched a six-year low against the U.S. dollar.
Investors drove the won to its weakest point since March 1990, led by local companies buying dollars to finance imports as South Korean exports faltered.

Analysts said further erosion in the currency could spur inflation, reinforcing a grim outlook for South Korea's economy, which has been pinched by a widening current account deficit and high interest rates.
"If the dollar rises further, there will be more of a burden to pay expensive imports and that could trigger inflationary pressure," said Han Sang-choon, analyst at the Daewoo Research Institute.
Dealers said intervention began shortly after the won hit a six-year low of 830.30 in mid-morning trading.
The Bank of Korea (BOK) demonstrated its resolve with at least three rounds of intervention before stabilising the unit around 829.50 in late afternoon trading, dealers said. It had opened at 829.70.
"The central bank's intention to support the won looks firm," said a dealer with a foreign bank.

Dealers said many investors, however, appeared fixed on defying the central bank and were likely to continue buying U.S. dollars given the grim outlook for the won and the prospects of rising dollar demand from importers.
"Most banks seem to prefer to build up dollar positions because of the slim possibility that dollar inflows by exporters would increase," said a dealer with a domestic bank.

South Korea's exporters, who usually help support the won, have been hit hard by a global slump in some of the country's major products, such as semiconductors, steel goods and petrochemical products.

Also weighing on the won has been a slide in the amount of offshore money landing in the South Korean stock market despite an increase in the ceiling for foreign stock ownership to 20 percent from 18 percent last week.
"About $550 million came in last week. But foreign funds began to go out this week," said Han of Daewoo.
He said expectations for a further rise in the dollar against the won had fuelled the outflow of funds.
"Given the dollar's rise, almost no one will want to hold the won in place of the dollar because of the expected loss from the foreign exchange translation," he said.
Over the longer term, analysts said pressure remained strong for the won to depreciate against the dollar to boost exports.

"The won-dollar rate should be between 830 and 840 in view of consumer prices and the status of international payments," said a analyst at the Hyundai Research Centre, referring to South Korea's $10 billion trade deficit last year.
The deficit is expected to double this year.
Dealers said the dollar's recent strength against the yen also helped push the U.S. currency higher against the won.
"If Japanese products became more competitive in overseas markets due to a low yen, the won should fall to boost the price advantage of South Korean products," a domestic dealer said.
